stem: A cancer survivor says, 'My follow-up scan is next week. I am so afraid the cancer is back that I am thinking about canceling the appointment.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Acknowledge the fear, assess how much it is affecting daily function and follow-up care, encourage the client to keep the recommended follow-up plan, and offer psychosocial support or counseling if needed.
options.B: Tell the client there is no reason to worry because completing treatment guarantees that the cancer will not recur.
options.C: Support canceling the scan because avoiding cancer-related reminders is the best way to reduce fear of recurrence.
options.D: Explain that fear of recurrence is abnormal after treatment and by itself proves the client has a psychiatric disorder.

rationale: A is correct. NCI describes fear of cancer recurrence as a common survivorship concern and notes that follow-up scans and other medical tests can trigger substantial anxiety or 'scanxiety.' NCI advises survivors to tell the healthcare team about recurrence fears, maintain follow-up care, and seek counseling when fear becomes more than they can manage. Psychosocial assessment should consider how distress affects functioning and care. B is incorrect because treatment completion does not guarantee that recurrence is impossible. C reinforces avoidance of recommended follow-up rather than addressing the fear. D incorrectly pathologizes a common survivorship concern without assessing its severity or impact.
educational_objective: Respond to fear of cancer recurrence by validating the concern, assessing its functional and care impact, supporting recommended follow-up, and facilitating psychosocial help when anxiety becomes difficult to manage.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Coping — Life After Cancer Treatment; Follow-Up Medical Care; Adjustment to Cancer: Anxiety and Distress (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version
source_version_date: Follow-Up Medical Care updated 2024-12-02; current NCI survivorship and PDQ resources accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: Life After Cancer Treatment — heading 'Coping with fear of cancer recurrence': fear of recurrence as a common concern, scan/follow-up triggers, telling the care team, follow-up care plan, and counseling when fears are difficult to manage; Follow-Up Medical Care — opening follow-up-care purpose and 'What to Tell Your Doctor during Follow-Up Visits' regarding emotional problems and new concerns; Adjustment to Cancer HP PDQ — 'Psychosocial Assessment' and survivorship/remission material addressing recurrence anxiety and functional impact of distress.
source_claim_supported: Fear of recurrence is common after treatment and may intensify around scans/follow-up; survivors should discuss it with the healthcare team, maintain follow-up care, and may need psychosocial support when fear interferes with coping or function.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Client Needs category 'Psychosocial Integrity' — nursing care that promotes and supports emotional, mental and social well-being; applied here to anxiety, coping, therapeutic communication, psychosocial assessment and referral during survivorship.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's definition-only recurrence-fear item into an applied survivorship scenario where anxiety threatens adherence to follow-up. The final item validates a common concern, assesses impact, protects continuity of surveillance and offers support without false reassurance or automatic psychiatric labeling.
audit_findings: Fresh NCI review directly supports fear of recurrence as common and follow-up scans as a trigger for anxiety.
NCI explicitly supports discussing fears with the care team, keeping a follow-up plan and obtaining counseling when fear is difficult to manage.
The final item assesses impact rather than diagnosing a psychiatric disorder from recurrence fear alone.
Distractors represent realistic errors: false cure guarantee, avoidance of recommended surveillance and inappropriate pathologizing.
Independent adversarial review found no second answer, cueing, unsupported recurrence claim, locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or unresolved conflict.
